subject: research/rank-elicitation
professional: a statistician / decision-theorist working on proper scoring rules and property elicitation (Lambert, Gneiting, Frongillo school), who would check first: is the score proper, is the regret algebra right, is the Brier comparison fair, and what is new relative to the property-elicitation literature

evidence.correctness: Ran `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` in research/rank-elicitation: 7 tests OK. Recomputed with a separate script (python3 -I, exact Fractions / raw Brier scores, no package code): (1) worst-case regret for p=(.4,.3,.15,.1,.05), equal weights, brute force over all 120 permutations = 9/20 = 0.45, matches the paper and results.txt E3; (2) adjacent-swap regret at gap 0.3, K=5: linear 3/40=0.075, Brier/range 9/100=0.09, ratio 0.8333, matches E1 (and crossover 1/(K-1) is algebraically right: d/(K-1) < d^2 iff d > 1/(K-1) for the linear score being weaker, so the stated direction holds); (3) detection n for the swap (.25,.15): computing the Brier loss difference from raw Brier scores of the swapped report gives n=105.535 and the rank-loss difference gives 105.535, matching the paper's 105.5 (code rounds the rank n up to 106); (4) geometric q=.8 K=6 min spacing 0.12185 matches E2 0.1218. All four agree. Caveat: the identity in (3) is a one-line consequence of both differences being scalar multiples of the same +1/-1/0 variable, so it is correct but not a finding.
evidence.completeness: Every claim in README/whitepaper maps to code: strict propriety (test_true_ranking_is_unique_argmin), adjacent-swap closed form (test_adjacent_swap_closed_form), equal spacing optimal (test_equal_spacing...), reversed ranking worst (test_max_regret_is_reversal), top-k set free (test_topk_set_elicited), detection equality (test_diff_stats...), crossover (test_crossover). experiments/run.py produces E1-E4 and results.txt matches the paper's quoted numbers (0.83x, 2.5x, 25x, 250x; 0.052/0.03 spacings; 106 vs 105.5). Paper, figure.py and ratio.svg present. No stubs or TODOs found. Not checked: the live page https://marisstella.app/research/rank-elicitation/ (outbound hosts not probed).
evidence.verification: Seeded mutation in src/rank_elicitation/model.py: detection_n changed from `z*z*var/(mean*mean)` to `z*var/(mean*mean)` (z not squared). Re-ran the 7 tests: still `OK` (SURVIVED). Cause: test_diff_stats_exact_and_detection_equal compares detection_n of the linear and Brier stats against each other, so a common bug in detection_n cancels; no test pins an absolute n (106). The mutation did change experiments/run.py output (n=65, sim power 0.33 instead of ~0.5), so the experiment script would show it, but nothing in the test suite fails. Reverted with git checkout; suite OK again, git status clean. Other core functions (regret, max regret, spacing) are tested against brute force and closed forms and would catch typical mutations; tests use seeded randomness and brute force over K<=6, which is a good design. Only 7 tests and one untested core function (swap_diff_stats_brier is compared only in one point; geometric_weights tested only through other tests).
evidence.craft: Read src/rank_elicitation/model.py (97 lines), __init__.py, tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, pyproject.toml. Small, stdlib-only, clear docstrings, no copied engines. Defects: `math` imported but unused in model.py; no input validation (K=1 divides by zero in equal_weights, p not on the simplex, mismatched lengths accepted silently); true_ranking breaks ties by index silently; geometric_weights with q=1 divides by zero; __all__ present. Tests do `from rank_elicitation import *`. No ruff/type hints. Acceptable for a research artefact, not a library.
evidence.claims: The README and paper checked claim by claim against code/results.txt: strictly proper for strictly decreasing w (tested K=3-5, 2 weight vectors, 90 truths); regret formula exact; equal spacing maximises min spacing (this is a one-line pigeonhole, tested at 3 values of q); linear beats Brier iff gap<1/(K-1) (checked algebraically above); worst = reversed (brute force). The paper itself says 'Standard rearrangement-inequality and polyhedral-score facts applied to this setting; not new theory', which is honest. Limits (risk-neutral, known truth, one report, per-unit-range comparison) are stated. Weak spots: 'the worst report is the reversed ranking' is asserted from rearrangement and tested only to K=6; the claim 'beats a Brier-derived ranking per unit payment range' compares a ranking report with a probability report whose range is dominated by magnitudes the ranking buyer does not want, so the headline ratio (250x) is a property of normalisation, which the paper partly concedes in Section 5. Expected payoff 'gain' numbers (0.0125-0.05 vs 0.01) are stated without a cost model. No disclaimer needed (not a product).
evidence.fitness: A researcher could reuse the closed forms and the 90-line module to design a payment for ranking tasks (routers / referees), but nothing here is a result beyond textbook: the score is a polyhedral/linear (weighted rank-position) scoring rule, whose properness for finite-valued properties is standard. Nearest prior work: Lambert, Pennock & Shoham 2008 'Eliciting properties of probability distributions' (EC); Lambert & Shoham 2009 'Eliciting truthful answers to multiple-choice questions' (EC; scoring for the mode/ordering of a categorical distribution); Lambert 2018 'Elicitation and evaluation of statistical forecasts' (rank/ordinal properties and their elicitability); Frongillo & Kash 2015 'On elicitation complexity'; Finocchiaro, Frongillo & Waggoner 2019-20 on polyhedral losses and surrogate regret (linear vs quadratic regret split); Gneiting 2011 'Making and evaluating point forecasts' (consistent scoring functions for ordinal/quantile properties); Ramaswamy, Tewari & Agarwal and Duchi, Mackey & Jordan on calibrated surrogates for ranking; Savage 1971. The whitepaper cites none of them (it cites only sibling projects in this repo). Novelty: not new, and the paper correctly does not claim to be; soundness: sound but small, with the regret/detection results being direct computations. Not publishable at a main-track venue; a worked note at best.
evidence.domain: A scoring-rule specialist would accept the algebra but would first ask for the literature position (missing), the fact that a rank-position loss 1-w[sigma(y)] elicits the *ordering of probabilities* only because it is a linear score in the indicator (so it is a known 'weighted-argmax-over-permutations' property), and would object that the per-range comparison with Brier is not the right benchmark: the right comparison is against other ranking-eliciting incentives (Spearman/Kendall-type losses of an elicited full ranking, top-k indicators, Lambert's multiple-choice scores) and against the information content (a ranking tells you less than the probabilities, so cheaper incentive is expected). The model also ignores verifier effort cost, risk aversion and noisy/unknown truth, which are what actually matter in a decentralised-ML verification setting; the 'expected payoff gain per task' and 'detection n' sections are then of limited decision value. The detection-sample-size result is z-test power arithmetic (and 'simulated power 0.50' is the target by construction at n=z^2 var/mean^2).

defects.what: Mutation survives: detection_n with z not squared passes all 7 tests, because the only detection test compares linear against Brier through the same function, so a shared bug cancels. No test pins an absolute value (e.g. n=106 for p=(.25,.15), K=any).

No citation of the elicitation / scoring-rule literature (Lambert-Pennock-Shoham 2008, Lambert-Shoham 2009, Lambert 2018, Finocchiaro et al., Gneiting 2011); the novelty position cannot be assessed from the paper, only from outside knowledge.

Headline 'up to 250x more incentive than Brier' is a normalisation artefact (ranking report vs probability report at equal payment range) and is not a comparison with other ranking-eliciting incentives; the benchmark is a strawman for the claim.
Unused import math; no input validation (K=1, q=1, non-simplex p, length mismatch); silent index tie-break in true_ranking.

E4 'simulated power' is ~0.5 by construction at n=z^2 var/mean^2, so the simulation checks only the normal approximation, not a result; detection equality for linear vs Brier is a scalar-multiple identity.

verdict: A small, correct, stdlib-only research note: the closed forms (adjacent-swap regret, reversed-ranking worst case, equal-spacing optimum, top-k set, detection n) all recomputed independently (exact fractions and raw Brier scores) and match the paper and results.txt, and the 7 tests pass. It is honest that it is not new theory, but it does not cite the property-elicitation literature a referee would expect, its headline 250x ratio is a normalisation artefact against a weak benchmark, and its tests missed a seeded bug in detection_n (z not squared), so verification is 2. Correctness, claims and craft reach 3, verification 2 and domain 2 mean it does not meet the bar; it is finished (completeness 3) but not a PhD-level programme result, and a practitioner would use the formulas as a reference, not as a research contribution.
